1.1.title: Clock Sync: Server Status
1.1.quest: Implement format_clock(host, offset_ms, synced). Return exactly "<id> | <offset_ms to 2 decimals> ms | SYNCED" (or DRIFTING when synced is False). Do not print instead of returning. Example: format_clock("web-1", 3.3, True) → "web-1 | 3.30 ms | SYNCED". Accept negative and zero offsets (a clock can run behind as well as ahead).
hints: Start with status = "SYNCED" if synced else "DRIFTING".
Use an f-string with {offset_ms:.2f}; spaces and punctuation are part of the contract.

0.title: Variables are labels
body: A **variable** is a name attached to a value — like a named entry in a config file. You create one with `=`.
Once a name exists you can reuse it anywhere below that line. Python reads your file from top to bottom.
0.code:
offset_ms = 3.3
host = "web-1"
synced = True
print(host, offset_ms, synced)
0.note: `=` stores a value. `==` asks a question ("are these equal?"). Mixing them up is the most common beginner bug.

1.title: Four basic types
body: Every value has a **type**. You will use these four constantly:
`int` — whole numbers like `42`. `float` — decimals like `3.3`. `str` — text in quotes like `"web-1"`. `bool` — `True` or `False`.
Quotes matter: `"3.3"` is text, `3.3` is a number. `type(x)` tells you what you have.

3.title: Functions are reusable commands
body: A **function** packages a piece of logic so you can reuse it. Parameters are the arguments you pass in; `return` is the result the command hands back.
The body is everything indented by four spaces under the `def` line. The function does nothing until you **call** it with parentheses.
3.code:
def double(x):
    result = x * 2
    return result

print(double(21))

6.title: Formatting numbers with f-strings
body: Put `f` before a string and you can drop values into it with `{}`.
After a colon you can add a **format spec**. `:.2f` means "show as a float with exactly 2 decimal places" — it rounds the display and leaves the original value alone.
6.code:
offset_ms = 3.14159
print(f"Offset = {offset_ms:.2f} ms")
print(f"Offset = {0:.2f} ms")
print(offset_ms)

7.title: Picking between two values
body: A **conditional expression** chooses one of two values in a single line: `A if condition else B`.
It is perfect for turning a bool into a label.
7.code:
synced = False
status = "SYNCED" if synced else "DRIFTING"
print(status)

8.explain: :.2f always shows exactly two decimals, padding with zeros when needed.

9.title: Your mission: format_clock
body: You will write `format_clock(host, offset_ms, synced)` and **return** one line of text. The exact shape is `<id> | <offset_ms with 2 decimals> ms | SYNCED` — or `DRIFTING` when `synced` is False. Every space and `|` counts.
Examples the tests will check: `format_clock("web-1", 3.3, True)` → `"web-1 | 3.30 ms | SYNCED"` and `format_clock("db", 0, False)` → `"db | 0.00 ms | DRIFTING"`. Negative values work the same way.
9.note: Next: a 3-question quiz on these ideas. Pass it and the Build step unlocks.

0.explanation: An f-string evaluates offset_ms and :.2f displays exactly two decimal places.

1.2.title: Latency Filter: Loops & Lists
1.2.quest: Implement filter_latencies(latencies, low, high). Return a new list containing latencies in the inclusive [low, high] range, in original order. Never mutate latencies. Raise ValueError when low > high.
hints: Check low > high before the loop, even when latencies is empty.
Create result = []; append only latencies satisfying low <= latency <= high.

0.title: Lists hold latencies in order
body: A **list** is an ordered sequence of measurements: `[10, 20, 30]`. Each item has an index, and indexing starts at **0**.
Negative indexes count from the end: `-1` is the last item. `len(latencies)` gives the item count.

1.title: for loops visit each item
body: A `for` loop runs its indented body once per item, binding the item to a name you choose.

2.explain: -1 refers to the last item in the list.

3.title: Conditions decide what passes
body: `if` runs its body only when the condition is True. Comparisons like `<`, `<=`, `==` produce bools.
Python lets you **chain** comparisons: `low <= x <= high` means "x is between low and high, including both ends" — like the healthy band on a monitoring dashboard.

4.title: Build a new list, keep the input intact
body: To filter, start with an empty list and `append` what you want to keep. The caller's original list stays unchanged.
Never delete items from a list while looping over it — the loop skips elements and the caller gets a surprise.

6.title: The compact version: comprehensions
body: A **list comprehension** expresses the same filter in one line: `[x for x in latencies if condition]`.
Write the loop version first if it helps you think — both are correct.
6.code:
latencies = [1, 2, 3, 4]
evens = [x for x in latencies if x % 2 == 0]
print(evens)

body: Write `filter_latencies(latencies, low, high)` returning a **new** list of latencies where `low <= latency <= high`, in the original order. Don't modify `latencies`. If `low > high`, raise `ValueError`. Example: `filter_latencies([-3, 0, 2, 5, 8], 0, 5)` → `[0, 2, 5]`. An empty input returns `[]`.

body: A **virtual environment** (`.venv`) is a separate sandbox for one project: its own Python packages, isolated from every other project.

4.title: Calling Gemini
body: The `google-genai` SDK gives you a client object. You ask it to generate content for a model and read `.text` from the response.
4.code:
from google import genai

client = genai.Client(api_key=key)
response = client.models.generate_content(
    model=model, contents="Explain DNS in one line")
print(response.text)
4.note: Only create a client inside a function — never at import time — so importing your file never touches the network.

5.title: Dependency injection: plug in a test fixture
body: If your function builds its own client, tests can't avoid the network. Instead accept an optional `client` parameter. Real use passes nothing; tests pass a fake with the same shape.
It's like testing against a mock server: swap the fake in and you can check the whole flow offline, for free.

0.title: HTTP in one page
body: Web services talk with **HTTP**. A client sends a **request** (a method such as `GET`, plus a path like `/server/7`); the server sends back a **response** (a status code plus a body, usually JSON).
Think of it as a remote call with a standard envelope: every request names an action (method), a resource (path) and may carry data (body).
0.code:
GET /server/web-1          ← request
200 OK                     ← response status
{"id": "web-1", "latency": 3.3}   ← response body

2.2.quest: Expose FastAPI app and POST /servers. Validate name is nonempty and cpu is between 0 and 100 inclusive. Return the validated name and cpu with HTTP 201.

0.title: POST sends a body
body: `GET` reads. `POST` sends data in the request **body**, usually JSON, for the server to process or store.

1.title: Pydantic: a type check at the door
body: A **Pydantic model** declares the fields you expect and their types. Data that doesn't fit is rejected before your code runs — like an API gateway that rejects a request with a missing field.
1.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Server(BaseModel):
    name: str
    cpu: float

s = Server(name="A", cpu=42)
print(s.cpu)

2.title: Constraints with Field
body: `Field` adds rules: `min_length=1` rejects empty text; `ge` / `le` mean greater-or-equal / less-or-equal (inclusive bounds).
2.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Server(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(min_length=1)
    cpu: float = Field(ge=0, le=100)

3.prompt: With `cpu: float = Field(ge=0, le=100)`, is `cpu=100` accepted?
options: Yes — le means ≤, so 100 is allowed
3.explain: ge and le are inclusive. gt and lt would be exclusive.

4.title: Models as route inputs
body: Use the model as a parameter type and FastAPI reads the JSON body into it. Invalid bodies get an automatic **422** response — your function never runs.
4.note: status_code=201 (Created) in the decorator changes the success code from the default 200.

options: The function runs with an empty name
5.explain: min_length=1 rejects the empty name during validation, before your function is called.

2.3.quest: Implement store_event(db_path, name, duration). Create events(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, duration REAL) if needed, insert using parameters, commit, and return total row count. Persist across calls.

0.title: A database in a file
body: **SQLite** is a full SQL database stored in a single file — built into Python, no server needed. Data survives after your program exits.
0.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect("ops.db")   # creates the file if needed

1.title: Tables define the schema
body: A table is like a spreadsheet with fixed, typed columns. `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` makes it only the first time.
`INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` gives each row an auto-numbered id.
1.code:
con.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS events (
        id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
        name TEXT,
        duration REAL
    )
""")

2.title: Insert with ? placeholders
body: Pass values separately using `?` placeholders. SQLite keeps data and instructions apart.
Building SQL with f-strings lets a malicious value like `x'); DROP TABLE events;--` become part of the command — that's **SQL injection**. The verification test tries exactly this.
2.code:
name, duration = "deploy", 3.3
con.execute("INSERT INTO events (name, duration) VALUES (?, ?)",
            (name, duration))

4.title: Reading back: SELECT
body: `SELECT` queries rows. `fetchone()` returns one row as a tuple; `fetchall()` returns a list of them. `COUNT(*)` counts rows.
4.code:
count = con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events").fetchone()[0]
print(count)

2.4.quest: Implement async fetch_latency(reader). Await reader() once and return {"latency": value}. Convert TimeoutError to FastAPI HTTPException(status_code=503, detail="Monitor unavailable"). Let other exceptions propagate.

0.title: Exceptions are warning flags
body: When something goes wrong Python **raises** an exception that travels up until someone catches it. `try` / `except` catches it.
Catch only what you know how to handle. `except TimeoutError:` is precise; a bare `except:` swallows everything, including your own bugs.

1.title: Translate at the boundary
body: Inside a web service, a low-level fault should become a meaningful HTTP response. FastAPI's `HTTPException` does that: raise it and FastAPI sends that status code and detail.
1.code:
from fastapi import HTTPException

raise HTTPException(status_code=503, detail="Monitor unavailable")
1.note: 503 means 'temporarily unavailable — try later'. It's the honest code when a dependency times out.

3.title: async and await
body: `async def` defines a **coroutine** — a function that can pause while waiting on slow I/O so other work can run. Inside it, `await` waits for another coroutine's result.
Calling an async function doesn't run it; it returns a coroutine object you must `await`.
3.code:
import asyncio

async def read_monitor():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)    # pretend I/O
    return 3.3

async def main():
    v = await read_monitor()
    print(v)

asyncio.run(main())

5.title: Putting it together
body: Await the slow call inside `try`, translate the one error you understand, and let everything else propagate so real bugs stay visible.

6.title: Your mission: fetch_latency
body: Write `async def fetch_latency(reader)`. Await `reader()` **once** and return `{"latency": value}`. If it raises `TimeoutError`, raise `HTTPException(status_code=503, detail="Monitor unavailable")` instead. Any other exception should propagate unchanged.

0.title: Why split documents?
body: AI retrieval works on small, searchable pieces called **chunks** rather than one huge document. A question then matches the few chunks that matter.
Like paging through a huge log file in overlapping blocks: each block is small enough to search on its own.

4.title: Cosine similarity
body: Divide the dot product by both norms: `dot(a, b) / (norm(a) * norm(b))`. The result depends only on direction.
`1` = same direction · `0` = perpendicular (unrelated) · `-1` = opposite. Scaling a vector doesn't change its score.
4.note: Like comparing two users' interest profiles by direction, ignoring how active each one is overall.

2.title: Adding entries: upsert
body: Each entry has a string **id**, the **document** text and its **embedding**. `upsert` inserts new ids and overwrites existing ones, so running your code twice doesn't duplicate data.
2.code:
notes.upsert(
    ids=["0", "1"],
    documents=["DNS resolves names", "TCP retransmits packets"],
    embeddings=[[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]],
)
2.note: Passing embeddings yourself means Chroma never downloads an embedding model.

4.title: Querying
body: `query` takes a **list** of query vectors and returns the nearest entries. Results are nested: one inner list per query.
4.output:
[['DNS resolves names', 'TCP retransmits packets']]
['DNS resolves names', 'TCP retransmits packets']

It's like an event loop: each result feeds the next decision.

1.title: History is memory
